title: Nobel winner Anne Carson prints the Greek poet Sappho with brackets where papyrus is torn
body: On 8 October 2026 the Canadian poet and classicist Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature, which the [Swedish Academy](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/literature/2026/press-release/) gave for work in “playful dialogue with the classical tradition”. Among her books, *If Not, Winter* (2002) translates Sappho, who lived on the Greek island of Lesbos around 600 BC. Sappho probably wrote about 10,000 lines, but only **about 650** survive, probably because when books moved from papyrus rolls to parchment pages, too few people had hers copied. What is left reached us in two ways: quoted by later writers, like the whole Ode to Aphrodite in a book by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, or on torn papyrus thrown away in ancient Egypt and dug up again, much of it from an old rubbish dump at Oxyrhynchus. Carson doesn’t fill the holes with guesses: she marks each gap with a square bracket and leaves white space, keeps Sappho’s word order, and adds no words that aren’t in the Greek. Her title comes from fragment 22, where the words “if not, winter” stand between gaps.

slides.question: The Greek poet Sappho probably wrote about 10,000 lines of poetry. Roughly how many survive today?
slides.explanation: About 650, roughly one line in fifteen. Only one of her poems, the Ode to Aphrodite, is certainly complete.

slides.alt: Animation on dark umber with cream papyrus: Anne Carson’s name and a book, 10,000 marks of which 650 stay lit, a papyrus roll beside a parchment book, a Greek quotation on a page, scraps rising from a rubbish mound in Egypt, and a page of brackets with the words if not, winter.

slides.prompt: Mark each syllable of this line by Sappho long or short, using the rules below, until it fits her metre. Then listen to it.
slides.takeaway: – ∪ – × – ∪ ∪ – ∪ – –, where × can be either: the Sapphic line of all 330 stanzas in her first book. With a fixed pattern, an editor facing a torn line can tell how many syllables are lost.

left.label: Quoted
left.text: Later writers copied lines into their own books. The critic Longinus quoted fragment 31; Dionysius of Halicarnassus quoted the whole Ode to Aphrodite.

right.label: Dug up
right.text: Torn papyrus thrown away in ancient Egypt, much of it found from the late 1800s in an old rubbish dump at Oxyrhynchus.

slides.question: In Anne Carson’s translation of Sappho, what does a square bracket ] stand for?
options: A gap where the Greek is lost
slides.explanation: She marks each place where the papyrus is torn or the text is lost, instead of guessing the missing words, and leaves white space around it.
